GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 5 / 57 Glossary and Terminology Term Description Adaptation Adaptation is any adjustment in natural or human systems in response to actual or expected climatic stimuli or their effects which moderates harm or exploits beneficial opportunities. Adaptation pathway Alternative term use: adaptation strategy Adaptation pathway is a sequence of measures in time to achieve a set pre - defined objectives under changing external changing conditions, such as climate, socio - economic factors or other developments.

IWRM IWRM is a cross‐sectoral approach at the core of UN - SDG6, designed to promote the coordinated development and management of water, land, and related resources to maximise economic and social welfare equitably, without compromising the sustainability of ecosystems and the environment Resilience Resilience is the capacity for a socio - ecological system to: (1) absorb stresses and maintain function in the face of external stresses imposed upon it (e.g. by climate change), and (2) adapt, reorganize, and evolve into more desirable configurations that improve the su stainability of the system, leaving it better prepared for future (climate change) stresses. Indicators (evaluation) Indicators express to what extent the objective has been achieved. As such, they are the measuring rod that show how successful a project (or project portfolio) has been.

Flexible (measures) Alternative term use: adaptive Flexible measures can be adapted ( e.g. intensification of the action), abandoned (switch to a different action) or extended (add an action) at relatively low cost or having small societal impact. Flexible actions do not result in lock - ins and have little influence on potential future options ( i.e. have less path - dependencies ). Lock - in Lock - in : Situation where some future measure in a pathway can only be implemented with associated high costs or high societal impact. Measure Alternative terms used: intervention, action A measure is a particular course of action. Types of measures are: technical (structural), ecological, economic, regulatory, institutional. Mi tigation Mitigation is reducing the flow of heat - trapping greenhouse gases into the atmosphere, either by reducing sources of th ese gases or enhancing the “sinks” that accumulate and store these gases.

Objective Alternatives used: goals, aim An objective defines what is to be achieved or how some target is to be met. Goals identify needs, prioritize issues and define targets and constraints on the actions to be taken to meet the targets. Goals may define preferred courses of action. For example, the goal might be to apply user - oriented demand management measures rather than relying on large - scale water supply infrastru cture development. Path dependency Path - dependency is the reduced flexibility between actions, due to the commitment to certain development trajectories and/or limited future alternatives to adapt to unforeseen changes. Path dependency may result from the legacy of the infrastructure and/or the associated economic and social developments triggered by the investment ( e.g., higher costs or limits).

GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 6 / 57 Decision path - dependency arises from sequencing decisions and scenario path - dependency arises from environment al or socio - economic changes in the operating environment (e.g., population growth reduces space to adapt). Robustness (of a system) The ability of a system to remain functioning under a large range of disturbance magnitudes (i.e., plausible scenario conditions ). Robust measures Robust measures and/or strategy: Measures that result in acceptable indicator values under a wide variety of futures. Scenario A scenario is defined as the environment exogenous to the water system under consideration that cannot be controlled by the decision maker involved. Socio - economic developments and climate change are the most important scenario components in water resources systems.

Strategy Alternatives used: plans, portfolio plan, portfolio of p rojects, policy, adaptation pathways Sometimes the term Scenario is used; this should be avoided as scenario’s describe external conditions A strategy is defined as a logical combination of individual measures or decisions that accomplishes the stated obje ctives and satisfies the constraints imposed on the water resources system. A strategy can be described in terms of (alternative) pathways . Water Resource System The Water Resource System (WRS) is the integrated system of the Natural Resource System (NRS), Socio - economic System (SES) and the Administrative and Institutional System (AIS) . Water security The vision for a paradigm shift in water security is to secure water resilience and water services under conditions of increased climate change impacts.

Water security is part of the health, food, and water security result area emphasises mostly adaptation projects to harness available w ater resources and develop resilient water infrastructures and services . Note: For an overview of general key terms as used by GCF, reference is made to the Glossary of the GCF Programming Manual .

GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 7 / 57 Executive summary Project proposals, submitted to GCF for funding, should be based on a climate rational, sound technical and economic analysis , innovation , as well must comply with the specific conditions of GCF. These guidelines provide practical information and recommend ations on how to prepare the technical content of water related project proposals. These guidelines are complementary to the Water Security Sector al Guide 1 that describes the position and ambitions of GCF in the water sector as well as the financial mecha nisms and implementation arrangements that GCF is willing to support. This document translates the Water Security Sector al Guide into how projects can be designed to be suitable for GCF to finance, because they meet GCF’s investment criteria. The specific GCF requirements and funding proposal template are described in the GCF Programming Manual.

The target audience of these guidelines are the Direct Access Entities and Accredited Entities. The guidelines might also be useful for International Access Entitie s, or any other organisation interested in accessing GCF funding. The technical analysis as described in these guidelines starts with recognizing the intricate connections between the natural resource system, the socio - economic system (the users of the wat er) and the administrative and institutional system. These connections require that water sector projects should follow an integrated approach to reduce climate risk . How much ‘integration’ is needed depends on the specific project, but each proposed water sector project should consider how the project might impact other users, sectors and the environment. Moreover, these Guidelines recommend a strong engagement of al l relevant stakeholders .

To ensure such integrated approach and the involvement of all stakeholders, a system based structured process of project design needs to be followed. GCF funding requires that project proposals have a clear climate rationale, in li ne with policy paper B.33/05 , to ensure that the project responds directly to climate change challenges. The climate rationale is embedded in the structured process of project design. This will provide the evidence of the impacts of climate change by ident ifying the hazards, exposure and vulnerability of the system under consideration. This risk analysis provides the information based upon which a set of alternative interventions can be formulated, and the preferred solution (the project/program) is selecte d and proposed to GCF for funding. GCF has adopted a four - pronged approach to accelerate and scale up climate innovation. The first prong focuses in establishing a conducive policy and institutional environment for climate solutions.

The second is to cat alyse and facilitate the emergence of climate innovation. The third is to use scarce public resources and de - risk investments that have potential to foster private finance. The fourth is to accelerate the widespread adoption of new climate solutions. Water is a cross - cutting with many other GCF climate sectors such as agriculture, food, forests, energy (hydropower), urban, ecosystems management and infrastructure. This document focusses on providing project design guidelines by establishing a structured pro cess and defining the main steps for project development (Part 1) and providing applications for IWRM and three water sub - sectors (Part 2 ), climate resilient WASH , d rought risk management and flood risk management. IWRM projects . Only IWRM projects (mainly focussed on adaptation) that include actual investments can be considered for regular GCF funding.

IWRM planning projects (such as river basin management and plans) and feasibility studies can be supported by GCF by means of GCF’s Readiness and Preparator y Support Program. IWRM projects eligible for GCF funding should include components that bring together water users from multiple sectors to co - invest in mutual benefits. This can include users from other sectors of GCF such as agriculture, food, forests, energy, urban, ecosystems management and infrastructure. Climate Resilient WASH projects. WASH projects should aim at improving the health, socio - economic situation and resilience of the communities involved preferably by addressing the whole WASH system ( cross - cutting project between adaptation and mitigation). GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 8 / 57 the WASH infrastructure and services sustainable, safe and resilient to climate - related risks. These resilient WASH systems should co ntribute to helping build community resilience to the impacts of climate change and by improving water and energy efficiency. In summary, these projects should deliver both mitigation ( e.g., hydropower or use of renewable energy for water production) and a daptation benefits. Drought Risk Management projects. Drought risk projects should aim to reduce the risk of communities to water shortages and to prevent severe economic, social and ecological impacts of droughts. GCF drought projects must address the exacerbation of drought due to climate change. Drought projects shoul d include an extensive analysis of the historical hydro - meteorological condition ( e.g., water availability , depth - duration, precipitation ) and the expected changes due to climate change.

Hydrological /hydraulic (1D - 2D) and/or water balance modelling might be required to assess the impact of climate on the users and to evaluate the effectiveness of interventions that aim to reduce the risk. Interventions can address the drought and other cascading risk and consequences . Nature Based Solutions (NBS) should be considered, where possible, as they are often cheaper and more sustainable. Also, consideration should be given to cross sectoral interventions, for instance water allocation across sectors incl uding priority settings, during drought events. Flood Risk M anagement projects. Flood projects should aim at reducing the impacts of flooding. GCF flood projects should address the increased risk of flooding (and related damage) due to climate change. As with drought projects this will require an extensive analysis of the historical hydrology and the expected impacts of climate change on the flooding situation.

Hydrological and hydro - dynamic models are needed to determine the potential flooding frequency and extent. These models, together with impact models (damages , benefits) are also needed to determine the effectiveness of interventions that aim to reduce the risk. Possible interventions should consider the full risk cascade and include the reduction of the hazard, increased protection, regulation of land - use, and the raising of awareness and preparedness. As with droughts, Nature Based Solutions are promising interventions in flood projects, both for hazard reduction as well as for protection against floods.

E.g., through demand management, smart digital water management, decentralized operation models and resource recovery. - Pathway 2 : Strengthen integrated water resources management – protection from water - related disasters, preserve water resou rces and enhanced resilient water supply and sanitation services. e.g., through Ecosystem - based management, alternative water sources and IWRM. It describes what is to be achieved. It also enforces many enablers to achieve the paradigm shifts that were identified in the Water Security Sectoral Guide. It is assumed that the guid elines will also be helpful for the International Access Entities (IAE) and/or useful to any organisation interested in accessing GCF funding for water projects. GCF water related activities are addressed at various levels. For these Guidelines we disting uish: 1. National Adaptation Plan (NAP). The NAP identifies medium - and long - term adaptation needs and developing and implementing strategies and programmes to address those needs. Water is often a prioritised sector in these NAPs. 2. Country programme .

Country programmes set out the country’s objectives for engaging with GCF and provide an indicative list of proposed projects (in various sectors, not only the water sector) that the country intends to submit for GCF funding. GCF encourages countries to develop a nd submit country programmes so that the linkages and priorities among projects of a particular country are clear. This is the responsibility of the NDA. 3. Water programme . A programme is defined here as a set of related projects and activities aimed at achieving one or more strategic objectives. An example is a wastewater recycling programme that provides on - lend funds to different municipalities in the same country, or a transboundary water management programme that funds interventions in different countries sharing a water resource. 4. Individual water ‘project’ .

A project is a set of activities carried out in a temporary partnership, aimed at achieving predefined results within certain preconditions ( e.g., time, money). These projects will often have specific requests for investments. This document addresses mainly the last two categories, ensuring that project proposals submitted to GCF for funding are technically sound and meet GCF’s investment framework. The first two categories might benefit from the Guidelines when identifying water - related projects to be included in their programmes and plans. Developing NAPs and Country Programs can be financed by GCF’s Readiness Pr ogramme 4 . Water is only one of several sectors under the eight results areas of the GCF. Due to the integrated nature of the water sector, there are many linkages with other GCF climate sectors such as agriculture, forests, energy (hydropower), urban, ec osystems management and infrastructure.

This document aims to support better project design, in particular the conceptualization of effective solutions to address climate change induced problems. These guidelines will support the stages 3 (Concept note su bmission) and 4 (Funding proposal development) in the Project cycle of GCF, as illustrated in Figure 3 . GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 13 / 57 1.3 Linking project indicators to investment criteria An additional consideration in designing a project is to give specific attention to GCF’s investment framework 7 . The GCF’s investment framework defines six investment criteria and related indicators that provide guidance in the development, assessment and approval of projects. They seek to promote consistency and transparency in funding proposals and promote efficiency in the assessment process. By enhancing the clarity of how funding proposals meet GCF investment criteria, these indicators can be used to enhance the quality of funding proposals. An overview of the GCF Investment criteria and how they can be advanced from a project design perspective is given below. The reader is directed to the specific GCF document 8 on this subject for a more detaile d description.

• Impact potential - Potential of the project or programme to contribute to the achievement of GCF's objectives and result areas. ➔ Impact potential relates mostly to the effectiveness of the proposed investments to reduce climate change impacts (e.g. expected change in loss of lives, values, livelihoods, etc) and lower GHG emissions. • Paradigm shift potential - Degree to which GCF can achieve sustainable development impact beyond a one - off project or programme investment through replicabi lity and scalability. ➔ Paradigm Shift potential basically asks for contribution of the proposed investments to either pathway 1 or 2, though specific projects might identify other paradigm shifts. • Sustainable development potential – Degree to which the acti ons align with national SDG priorities and deliver wider benefits and priorities. ➔ For proper project design relevant co - benefits in economics, social, environment and gender empowerment should be part of the assessment.

• Needs of the recipient – Vulnerabil ity and financing needs of the country and population. ➔ For project design this means that a vulnerability analysis is needed to identify priority areas for interventions. A description of financial, economic, social and institutional needs and the barriers to access sources of climate - related finance is also required. • Country ownership - Beneficiary country ownership of, and capacity to implement, a funded project or programme (policies, climate strategies and institutions). ➔ The final project design should be aligned with N DC s, relevant national plans, indicators, and/or enabling policy and institutional frameworks. It should be explained how engagement of relevant stakeholders will increase ownership.

• Efficiency and effectiveness - Economic and, if appropri ate, financial soundness of the programme/project: Does the project foster cost - effectiveness and private sector funding mobilisation? ➔ These GCF criteria go beyond the more regularly used definitions of effectiveness and efficiency in project design. Indee d, the project needs to be effective in delivering impact (impact potential) against low net costs. But in addition, it is important to seek an optimal ratio of co - financing (concessional, private sector contribution), expected rate of return, and applicat ion of best practices. ———————————— —— 7 https://www.greenclimate.fund/projects/investment - framework 8 https://w ww.greenclimate.fund/sites/default/files/document/investment - criteria - indicators.pdf and https://www.greenclimate.fund/projects/criteria

1.4 Structure of this document The GCF Water project design guidelines consist of two parts: - Part 1 (the current document) provides generic practical guidelines and a stepwise approach for project design that meets GCF requirements - Part 2 (complementary document) provides additional context and guidance for when applying the guidelines to specific water sub - sectors as identified by GCF: Integ rated Water Resource Management (IWRM), Climate Resilient (CR) WASH, Drought Management and Flood Management. This document, Part 1, is structured as follows: chapter 2 describes the main elements for a GCF project proposal design with specific emphasis on the climate rationale, before chapter 3 elaborates the structured stepwise approach for project design. .

GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 15 / 57 2 Developing a n impact ful water programme or project for GCF financing This document describes how to design a project in such a way that will become eligible for GCF funding. The activities needed for designing a good project can be substantial, depending on the size and complexity of the project. Studies needed to design a project can be financed by GCF’s Project Preparation Facility. This chapter describes in section 2.1 the key principles for developing an impactful water project eligible for GCF funding. Section 2.2 outlines the climate rationale needing to be included in the project proposal. This section also describes the recommended risk - based approach to be applied, in particular for projects focused on dealing with strong climate variability (such as drought and flood risk projects). Section 2.3 explains the link b etween the proposed project or programme with the country’s NAP and NDC’s.

Finally, Section 2.4 describes how to use this guide. 2.1 Key principles for develop ing a n impactful water sector project Although each project is unique in scope and conditions, there are several key principles that need to be considered in developing a good water sector project: • the project should be ‘owned’ by the stakeholders (country ownership) • the project should take a n integrated view on the water system , hydrological cycle and climate risk reduction ; and • project formulation should follow a structured process with k ey checks and balances . 2.1.1 Ownership of project – stakeholder involvement The first condition is that the project is owned by key stakeholders, i.e., the beneficiaries of the project as well as the implementing partners. For this a participatory approach in developing and implementing the project is needed.

One of the first step s in the design of a project is to carry out a stakeholder mapping in which the beneficiaries are identified (and their wishes) as well as the implementing partners (and their mandates). The project design should be viewed as an interactive process of stak eholder engagement, that works towards a shared perception of the problems and solutions. In this process any ambiguity on what precisely are the problems, objectives and strategies is transformed into a shared perception on these topics and ultimately the formulated project. A process of joint fact finding with frequent interactions will also help to create a common knowledge base and a common view on the system to be studied. A shared perception of problems and potential solutions will also promote owners hip of the project to be developed. Figure 5 illustrates this process. Which stakeholders to involve depends on the problem and the project that is proposed.

The many interactions between components in the water system (see section 2.1.2 ) causes that each intervention in the system (a project) can impact many people and interests, also outside the water sector. This includes: - Other governmental agencies such as ministr ies or departments at the same governmental level (horizontal coordination) as well as higher or lower governmental levels (vertical coordination). - Direct users (such as water user associations and the private sector), but also upstream and downstream use rs of the proposed project site. Attention should be given to make the stakeholder process socially inclusive, improving the ability, opportunity, and dignity of those disadvantaged based on their identity (gender, age, minority groups, etc.). More inform ation on stakeholder engagement will be given in section 3.3.2 .

GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 16 / 57 Figure 5 : Engagement of stakeholders in project design Involving the stakeholders in project design is not only needed to build stakeholder ownership of the proposed project. Stakeholders, and in particular the people that are dependent on the water system, have a lot of k nowledge on that system, its problems and possible solutions. Making use of this (indigenous and local) knowledge will enhance the quality of the project design. Indigenous knowledge built through generations can play a significant role in facing contempor ary challenges and may reveal improved solutions to climate adaptation and mitigation. 2.1.2 Integrated approach – take a systems perspective The integrated character of water management requires that a good water project considers all interactions and cascading impacts that it may have with other components of the Water Resources System (WRS).

Even if the project is developed for a specific purpose (such as a wastewater treatment plant), it must also consider the impacts the project will have on other system com ponents. Such an integrated view on the WRS is illustrated in Figure 6 that identifies three sub - systems: the Natural Resource System (NRS), the Socio - Economic System (SES), and the Administrative and Institutional system (AIS). The figure also shows the r elations that exist between these sub - systems. Considering all these sub - systems with their interrelationships is at the heart of Integrated Water Resource Management (IWRM). GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 17 / 57 The natural resource system (NRS) consists of the streams, rivers, lakes and their embankments and bottoms, the groundwater aquifers, and the water itself. This includes the abiotic (or physical), biological, and chemical (‘ABC’) components in and above the soil. It also includes the infr astructure needed to collect, store, treat and transport water such as canals, reservoirs, dams, weirs, sluices, wells, pumping stations, pipes, sewers, and water and wastewater treatment plants, and the policies or rules for operating them. The socio - econ omic system (SES) comprises the water - using and water - related human activities. This component can also include the stakeholders, i.e., the interested and affected public. The administrative and institutional system (AIS) comprises the institutions that a re responsible for the administration, legislation, and regulation of the supply (NRS) and demand (SES) components.

The AIS includes all institutions that plan, build and operate the infrastructure required for water security. This includes both soft (regu lations, policies, acts, laws, etc.) and hard (organisation, governance, structure, etc.) institutions, but may also include informal institutions such as community groups, volunteer networks, etc. All these systems and their interactions should be conside red during project design. The level of detail for their analysis depends on the specific project and how much it will interact with the different system components, i.e. the project’s footprint or area of influence . 2.1.3 Structure d Process in Project Design The project proposal should provide specific information on the project for which funding is requested. This includes a description of its objective (i.e. the problem that it is trying to address) and socio - economic context. It should explain why that spe cific project is proposed and not an alternative.

Moreover, it should describe how the project will be implemented. A specific condition for GCF projects is that the project should be designed to address problems caused by climate change (see section 2.2.1 ) . A common analytical approach for the development of a project or programme is given in Figure 7. It distinguishes four phases, each with its own focus. The first three phases prepare and design the project. The resulting ‘project’ is then translated int o an action (investment) plan in the fourth phase. A generic description of this Framework for Analysis is given in Deltares, 2021 10 . The four phases are described in detail in the next chapter. Each phase describes a specific part of the project design process. Climate change and building climate resilience must receive specific attention in all phases, including: • Scoping/Decision context. Setting the objectives and assessment indicators should demonstrate a clear focus on enhancing climate resili ence or mitigation.

If appropriate, a link with the National Adaptation Plan and the National Determined Contributions should be made. • Situation analysis/Climate science base. During the scenario and/or risk assessment for the current and future situation ( i.e., without taking actions) a range of climate change scenarios/projections must be analysed alongside socio - economic developments. By assessing these both individually and in combination, the additional contribution of climate change to any potential i mpacts can be assessed. ———————————— —— 10 Deltares, 2021. Taking longer term climate change impacts into account during early stages of the analysis may result in the promotion of measures that are more flexible and/or robust to the uncertainties involved than ‘traditiona l’ BAU measures. Climate risk assessment will be key element to design adaptation pathway. Adaptation pathways, or sequenced strategies commencing with more flexible, low - regret options to which extra robustness may be added over time, may need to be devel oped. Often, measures yielding additional mitigation benefits will emerge as low - regret. • Action planning. Traditionally, the water sector is mostly funded by public institutions or governmental organizations. Climate change might bring in other financial players including the private sector; for example, local businesses also have a growing interest in safeguarding their water supply under changing conditions.

A co - investment approach opens new business cases for the implementation of measures. 2.2 Climate Rationale in project design GCF is mandated to expand collective human action to specifically respond to climate change. For GCF funding, projects should response to issues induced or enhanced by the changing climate. This needs to be demonstrated by the climate rationale, as an essential integrated part of the entire project design to support a country’s NDC and NAP. 2.2.1 Climate rationale for GCF funding Figure 8 : Conceptual framework for guidance, selection and a ssessment of a GCF adaptation proposal Source: https://www.greenclimate.fund/sites/default/files/document/gcf - b33 - 05.pdf The overarching goal of GCF adaptation proposals is that they align with the global goal on adaptation (Article 7.1 of the Paris Agreement) of “e nhancing adaptive capacity, strengthening resilience and reducing vulnerability to climate change”.

Therefore, all proposals should in some way demonstrate how they achieve this or provide the “climate rationale ” for the intended project. To create a bette r common understanding of how to formulate a climate rationale, GCF has published a policy paper 11 . This policy paper proposes that the inclusion of a climate rationale ensures that projects are designed to address climate change. It can be thought of as t he overarching narrative that contributes to all GCF investment criteria (especially Impact Potential). For future climate, the uncertainties can be expressed by a range of possible climate projections or scenarios 12 . Using climate projections or scenarios Climate change modifies the characteristics of the historic climate.

The extent and way these modifications may take place are projected by Global Circulation Models (GCMs) that simulate coupled atmospheric - oceanic processes determining the earth’s climate. The most well - known global effort of standardization and inte rcomparison of the experiments carried out with these GCMs is the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP5 [1] , CMIP6). From CMIP5 and the CMIP6, climate projections of all IPCC emissions scenarios (coupled to potential socio - economic pathways) are ava ilable for users world - wide.

These climate projections can be used in multiple ways for water sector climate performance or risk assessment: • Directly as input to water system / hazard models • As a delta - change applied to the historic records that are used i n the analysis. That linkage can have two directions. The first direction is that the proposed project is part of the NAP as a concrete action. For GCF, this link is important as it indicates the ownership of the country over the proposed project.

The link also provides evidence that the project is aligned with other strategic deve lopments in the country. The other direction is that the project contributes to make the NAP and NDCs more concrete in terms of programming and specification. While the need to address climate change through water is well recognized, this is not always b eing translated into concrete action in most NDCs and NAPs. In the NDCs submitted by countries as part of the Paris Agreement, water is, in many cases, recognized in terms of policy statements or broad strategies – usually in terms of adaptation. But few N DCs have included the intention to prepare a specific water portfolio. And while most countries acknowledge water in their NDC’s ‘portfolio of actions’, few have estimated the related costs of these actions, even fewer have included detailed water - related project proposals. The project proposals as submitted to GCF can make this more concrete.

Natural Resources System (NRS) The NRS comprises the natural and engineered infrastructure, including the hydro - meteorological boundary conditions. For the SES also models can be used to quantify these demands and impacts.

The SES analysis provides information on the v ulnerability of the system to changing conditions. For GCF funding proposals, specific attention must be given to the impacts that climate change might have on people, livelihoods, and how those impacts are distributed . Administrative and Institutional Sys tem (AIS) An analysis of the AIS is required to identify any legal, regulatory, or institutional constraints on climate - resilient water resources management. Attention must be given to the interaction between various authorities involved in climate - resilie nt water resources management such as water resources management, disaster risk management, agriculture, environment, and hydrometeorology and to the effectiveness of their interactions. Systems perspective Problems related to the systems perspective have a focus on dealing with average conditions: to provide sufficient supply to meet the needs of the SES, to ensure that the water quality is acceptable, etc. IWRM and WASH projects usually address the systems perspective. Important elements are the water balance (demand versus supply) and water quality (mass balance of pollutants) .

Risk perspective The risk perspective has a focus on the extreme events and is in particular relevant for projects with a strong Disaster Risk Management (DRM) orientation such as floods and drought management. The risks involved include present risk (due to climate variab ility) and future risk (in which climate change will change climate parameters). The risk approach includes defining the (probability of the) event, the exposure, and the vulnerability, as explained in section 2.2.3 . The problem can be formulated at full risk level (e.g., expected damage with a certain return period) or separately for the different components of risk targeting specific vulnerability or exposure reducti on objectives (e.g., number of citizens exposed to hazards, coping capacity built among a number of organizations). It is noted that all projects will have systems and risk dimensions.

Also, in ‘systems’ projects it will be needed to include the risks ass ociated with climate variability and climate change. The difference is in the attention that need to be given to the risk dimension. The analysis of risk will be very prominent in flood and drought projects and will get less attention in the case of IWRM a nd WASH projects . Measures can be divided into different categories: technical (investment), m anagerial, economic, ecological, and institutional. An inventory of all possible kinds of actions that can be taken will in general result in a long list of possibilities. In most cases it will not be practicable to analyse all of these in detail. A screening process is needed to select the most promising ones. Screening is a rapid and global evaluation of possible actions in comparison with a more thorough evaluation under step III.3 (see section 3.5.3 ). This can be done in several ways. It can be done by using the modelling framework developed for the project, but it can also be done by limiting the analysis to a few indicato rs, such as economic benefit or environmental or social impact.

Best practice also suggests including an indication of the robustness and the flexibility of the proposed measures under the range of climate change uncertainty. Another kind of screening anal ysis is to apply expert judgment to evaluation criteria in line with the GCF investment criteria (see also section 1.3 ). Evaluation of project activities is also necessary to assess the expected performance against investment criteria (concept note part B. 3 and funding proposal part D). Formulation of the project - components and activities 3.5.1 Step III. 1 Design of alternative project s and impact assessment The design of a project or project portfolio involves the development of coherent combinations of promising measures to contribute to the achievement of the development objectives as formulated in Phase I and meet the targets as much as possible. As there are generally many indicators related to these objectives, and probably many of these objectives are expressed in different units, the design of projects is not a simple process.

Relationships among combinations of measures and their impacts on the evaluation indicators are complex. The optimum combination may depend on who is asked. Trade - offs among the values of different indicators, and disagreements among various stakeholders, are inevitable. It should also be considered that the implementation time of measures will differ.

GCF Water Project Design Guidelines Part 1 | 21 February 202 3 Page 42 / 57 The design of a project or project portfolio is therefore an iterative process. One approach is to start by developing a project based on one of the more important objectives and develop alternatives around th at first project design. These alternatives are defined by the boundaries of the solution space. Comparison of the economic benefits and the strategic environmental and social impacts of these alternatives can then lead to the construction of a compromise project by varying elements in the project. A resulting loss with respect to one criterion can then be compared with gains to another. Climate resilient water security project design is an ‘art’ rather than a science and requires good insight into the func tioning of the water system, the socio - economic requirements and impacts, and stakeholders’ preferences.

Project selection is often the result of negotiated interests and reflections on different views on how development should take place. The data and mod elling tools can help determine the expected economic benefits and strategic environmental and social impacts of the project in terms of the defined indicators. In case models are not available, the impacts can be estimated by experts. These estimates must be confirmed and accepted by the stakeholders and decision makers in workshops. The measures considered in this phase of the analysis are mostly at pre - feasibility level and can be added to the concept note formulation. In Phase IV - Action Planning, th e selected measures will be worked out in more detail, including possible design and feasibility studies. In that phase also an ESIA (Environmental and Social Impact Assessment) might need to be carried out, which is necessary for developing a robust fundi ng proposal.

As climate change raises threats of harm to human health and the environment, the precautionary principle should be applied in project design and preventive actions should be taken, even if some cause - effect relationships are not yet fully sc ientifically proven. According to the precautionary principle, uncertainty about the damage to be incurred should not serve as an argument to delay action. In the face of great uncertainty, a precautionary approach might result in a more stringent adaptati on response . 3.5.2 Step III.2 Dealing with uncertainty - adaptive management analysis The ultimate challenge is to make better informed decisions in water management under future uncertainties. Methods are available to make sure that the decision - making results into consistent, replicable, and accessible outcomes. The CRIDA (Climate Risk Informed Decision Analysis) approach might be employed to prepare such informed decisions 32 .

CRIDA is an approach that implements decision scaling and bot tom - up vulnerability approaches through collaborative stepwise planning procedures and Adaptation Pathways. The CRIDA approach incorporates both the Decision Tree Framework and Dynamic Adaptation Policy Pathways . The Decision Tree Framework 33 is a repeata ble process for the evaluation of climate change risks to new development projects. At the conclusion of this process, the project planner will be empowered to confidently communicate the method by which the vulnerabilities of the project have been assesse d, and how the adjustments that were made (if any were necessary) improved the project’s feasibility and profitability. The framework adopts a ‘bottom - up’ approach to risk assessment that aims at a thorough understanding of a project’s vulnerabilities to c limate change in the context of other non - climate uncertainties (for example, economic, environmental, demographic, or political).

It helps to identify projects that perform well across a wide range of potential future climate conditions, as opposed to see king solutions that are optimal in expected conditions but fragile to conditions deviating from the expected . The Strategic Framework for Climate Resilient WASH Development 34 advances sector thinking around WASH and climate change. The Framework is grounded in a core objective: to provide sustainable WASH service delivery, both now and into the future. The emphasis is on climate resilient development, including strengthening t he resilience of WASH systems and on investments to manage current climate variability, as well as long - term changes in climate. Different levels of analysis can be distinguished in terms of methods and techniques to be applied depending on the need of the case. Which one to use can be determined by answering the following questions : • Should future uncertainties be included in the analysis? • Is it beneficial to use the adaptation pathways approach? • Which economic evaluation method under uncertainty should be used?

These questions are not e asy to answer and the methods on how to deal with uncertainty in project evaluation are still developing. The need for these methods is growing, given the high uncertainty of climate change and the large impacts involved. For projects that require large in vestments (such as the construction of reservoirs) an adaptive pathway approach is strongly recommended. On the other hand, it should be recognised that these methods are very useful for countries with advanced management systems and access to a lot of rel iable data. If these are not available projects should be assessed and prioritized through a multi - criteria assessment that includes criteria such as ‘robustness’ and ‘flexibility’ . 3.5.3 Step III.3 Evaluation and ranking of alternative projects and decision - making Presentation of the selected promising projects to decision - makers may be done by means of briefings, presentations, and summary reports.

An issue with these methods is that the outcome depends on the methods cho sen. As part of the MCEM analysis a SWOT analysis can be carried out. The SWOT identifies the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats of each project.

Strengths and weaknesses are related to internal factors of the project that can make i t more likely to respectively succeed or fail. Whereas opportunities and threats are related to external factors that could help or harm project implementation. A SWOT analysis is a tool to be used to identify opportunities for project improvements . A cos t - benefit analysis (CBA) is another potential tool available to help ‘rank’ alternatives. It is a technique that considers monetary and non - monetary measures and helps decision - makers to design or choose the best alternatives within a project plan. It dete rmines how well or not a project may turn out. A social component can be added to the CBA, which is important because it comprises not just the financial effects of a project but also the social impacts such as pollution, drought, flood, employment rates, legal aspects, and many other impacts.

It is a tool to investigate the strong and weak points of alternatives, and to select the most viable projects, considering their socio - economic impacts. The analysis relies on summing positive factors and subtracting negative ones to determine a net result. When a project’s costs are less than the benefits derived from it, it is considered positive and viable. When the benefits derived do not compensate the planned financial investments, it is considered financially n on - viable and negative.

This is the money that has to be repaid over time (by the users or government ) . Developing the financial arrangements for a project is a specialized activity which is beyond the scope of these water project design guidelines. Reference is made to handbooks on this subject such as the Hand book for the implementation of Nature - based Solutions for Water Security 37 . The funding of a project could be either public or private. In general terms the main sources of funding are what the OECD calls the 3 T’s: Taxes, Tariffs or Transfers. The two mai n options to pay for the investments made are the taxpayers or the users.

As water related infrastructure and water management projects are generally considered public goods, they are normally financed by public funds (taxes). Depending on the type of proj ect and whether the project sponsor is public or private, a variety of financing instruments could be used for mustering the up - front resources needed such as loans, bonds and others. These are to be repaid by the funding over time. Government departments can allocate budgets to the implementation. Beneficiaries might pay a tariff for the service introduced. Specific donors and/or international development agencies might be interested to fund the measure under specific models ( e.g., 100% grant for part or f ull costs, or grant only for project preparation, etc.).
